planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring; in zone 9 plant March-May. Golden Star tolerates cooler nights slightly better than some Malaysian carambola selections but young wood is still damaged below 30F, so choose the warmest microclimate available in zone 9a.

directions: Golden Star was released from the University of Florida's Tropical Research and Education Center in the 1960s and remains grown for its large, deeply lobed fruit with an intense gold-orange color at full ripeness. Compared to the sweeter Arkin, Golden Star carries more acidity when picked early, so allow fruit to color fully on the tree before harvest to mellow the tartness into a balanced sweet-tart flavor good for fresh eating and juicing. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and irrigate consistently through bloom and fruit set, since irregular watering increases fruit drop and cracking. The tree bears on new growth flushes and can produce two overlapping crops per year in warm zones.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension -- Carambola Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
University of Florida Tropical Research and Education Center -- Carambola Cultivar Trials
California Rare Fruit Growers -- Carambola Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring; in zone 9 plant March-May. Carambola wood is frost-tender below 30F and established trees can be killed near 25F, so site Thayer in the most sheltered, frost-free spot available.

directions: Thayer is an older Florida carambola selection valued more for reliable vigor and disease tolerance than for exceptional fruit size, producing a steady crop of medium, ribbed, yellow-gold fruit with a mild, tart-sweet flavor that improves with full ripening on the tree. It is a useful pollinizer and dooryard tree where growers want production insurance alongside sweeter dessert cultivars like Arkin. Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, water deeply and consistently during dry spells, and prune lightly after each harvest flush to keep fruiting wood within reach. Fertilize several times a year with a balanced fruit-tree formula, as carambola is a heavy feeder relative to its modest size.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension -- Carambola Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
University of Florida Tropical Research and Education Center -- Carambola Cultivar Trials
Louisiana State University AgCenter -- Star Fruit for Gulf Coast

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring; in zone 9 plant March-May. Dah Pon is no more cold-hardy than other carambola selections and needs frost-free siting through its first several winters.

directions: Dah Pon is a Taiwanese-origin carambola cultivar grown for large, chunky, deeply five-ribbed fruit that is sweeter and less acidic than many older selections, making it popular for fresh slicing without the tartness some carambola varieties need time to lose. Trees are moderately vigorous and productive, flowering on new flushes several times a year in frost-free climates. Grow in full sun in deep, well-drained soil, maintaining even soil moisture through flowering and fruit fill to reduce fruit drop, and thin heavy fruit clusters if branches begin to bend excessively under the load.
sources: University of Florida Tropical Research and Education Center -- Carambola Cultivar Trials
California Rare Fruit Growers -- Carambola Fruit Facts
Taiwan Agricultural Research Institute -- Carambola Variety Notes

planting.note: Plant grafted container-grown trees in spring in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; damaged by temperatures below 30F, best suited to zone 10-12 in the ground.

directions: The purple-skinned form of star apple is the more widely traded of the two color types, prized for its glossy, deep violet rind that ripens to nearly black and encloses sweet, milky, translucent flesh; when sliced crosswise the seed cavities form the pale star pattern that gives the fruit its name. Purple-fruited selections tend to have a denser, slightly firmer texture than the green form and travel a bit better after picking. Grow in full sun on fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil, and pick when the skin develops a uniform dull sheen and yields slightly to gentle pressure, since fruit does not ripen further once removed from the tree. Grafted trees typically begin bearing within 3-5 years.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension -- Star Apple
Morton, 'Fruits of Warm Climates'
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden -- Star Apple Variety Notes

planting.note: Plant grafted container-grown trees in spring in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; damaged by temperatures below 30F, best suited to zone 10-12 in the ground.

directions: The green-skinned form of star apple ripens to a pale yellow-green rather than turning purple, with thinner skin and a softer, juicier interior than the purple type, though the flavor of the two color forms is essentially identical -- a mild, sweet, milky sweetness. Because the ripe green fruit shows little color change, growers judge ripeness mainly by a slight softening and a faint waxy bloom on the skin rather than by color shift. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil with consistent moisture, and handle ripe fruit gently since the thinner skin bruises more readily than the purple form. Grafted trees typically begin bearing within 3-5 years and produce over a long summer harvest window.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension -- Star Apple
Morton, 'Fruits of Warm Climates'
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden -- Star Apple Variety Notes

planting.note: Plant air-layered or grafted trees in spring; in zone 9 plant March-May. Like other longan, Sri Chompoo needs a brief cool-dry period below 59F to trigger flowering, which occurs naturally in zone 9 winters. Protect young trees below 30F.

directions: Sri Chompoo, also called Chompoo, is a Thai longan cultivar named for the faint pink blush of its aril -- an unusual trait among longan, which is normally translucent white throughout. The fruit is medium-sized with light brown, slightly rough skin, a small seed, and thick, aromatic, sweet flesh that many growers rate above standard cultivars for eating quality. Grow in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile soil, allowing the tree a period of relative dryness and cool nights in winter to encourage strong flowering the following spring. As with all longan, avoid heavy nitrogen fertilization during the winter chilling period, since lush new growth in place of flower buds is a common problem in overfed trees.
sources: University of Hawaii CTAHR -- Longan Production Guide
University of Florida IFAS Extension -- Longan Production in Florida
TFNet (International Tropical Fruits Network) -- Longan Varieties

planting.note: Plant air-layered or grafted trees in spring; in zone 9 plant March-May. Baidum needs the same brief winter chilling below 59F as other longan cultivars to set flowers reliably; protect young trees below 30F.

directions: Baidum, meaning 'black leaf' in Thai, is named for its distinctively dark, near-black young foliage and has become one of the most widely planted longan cultivars in Thailand, prized for consistently sweet, exceptionally aromatic white flesh and reliable heavy cropping. Fruit typically ripens in midsummer with a thin, tan-brown shell that peels away cleanly from a large, sweet aril. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, watering deeply during fruit development but allowing a drier, cooler rest period in winter to promote flower induction. Baidum trees are vigorous and benefit from annual pruning after harvest to maintain a manageable, well-lit canopy for the next season's crop.
sources: University of Hawaii CTAHR -- Longan Production Guide
TFNet (International Tropical Fruits Network) -- Longan Varieties
PROSEA (Plant Resources of South-East Asia) -- Dimocarpus longan

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun sheltered from strong wind; Seematjan is an Indonesian rambutan cultivar with soft, juicy flesh that is a favorite dessert type in Java.

directions: Seematjan is a long-established Indonesian rambutan cultivar from Java, grown for medium-sized, red, softly spined fruit with sweet, very juicy, easily separating flesh -- a texture many growers rate above the firmer commercial exports like Rongrien. It is an older selection that has been a dooryard favorite for generations but is less commonly grown commercially outside Southeast Asia because the soft fruit bruises and ships poorly. Plant grafted trees in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with shelter from wind, and keep soil evenly moist through flowering and fruit development, since rambutan is intolerant of drought stress at any life stage. Like all rambutan, Seematjan is strictly tropical and has essentially no frost tolerance.
sources: PROSEA (Plant Resources of South-East Asia) -- Nephelium lappaceum
TFNet (International Tropical Fruits Network) -- Rambutan Varieties
California Rare Fruit Growers -- Rambutan Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun sheltered from strong wind; Rapiah is a leading Indonesian rambutan cultivar valued for its sweet, low-moisture, semi-dry flesh.

directions: Rapiah has been one of the dominant rambutan cultivars planted in Java since the 1930s, distinguished from most other cultivars by unusually dry, firm, sweet flesh with lower juice content, which some growers prefer for out-of-hand eating because it separates cleanly from the seed with little mess. Fruit is medium-sized with soft red spines and a mild, consistently sweet flavor. Plant grafted trees in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with wind protection, providing steady irrigation through bloom and fruit fill despite the cultivar's drier flesh, since the tree itself still requires abundant moisture to crop well. Rapiah has no cold tolerance and is limited to the warmest, most humid tropical and near-tropical sites.
sources: PROSEA (Plant Resources of South-East Asia) -- Nephelium lappaceum
TFNet (International Tropical Fruits Network) -- Rambutan Varieties
California Rare Fruit Growers -- Rambutan Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun sheltered from strong wind; Simacan is a traditional Javanese rambutan cultivar grown alongside Rapiah in Indonesian nurseries since the 1930s.

directions: Simacan is a long-standing Javanese rambutan cultivar, historically one of the two dominant selections (alongside Rapiah) planted in Indonesian home orchards since the 1930s. Fruit is medium to large with red skin and soft spines, and the flesh is juicy and sweet with good separation from the seed. Grow grafted trees in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun sheltered from strong wind, and maintain consistent soil moisture year-round, since even brief drought during flowering can cause significant fruit drop. Simacan requires warm, humid, essentially frost-free conditions and is best suited to zone 10b and warmer in the continental United States.
sources: PROSEA (Plant Resources of South-East Asia) -- Nephelium lappaceum
TFNet (International Tropical Fruits Network) -- Rambutan Varieties

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in a humid, frost-free tropical climate; Musang King, registered in Malaysia as clone D197, requires the same consistent warmth above 50F as other durian and is realistically limited to the most tropical microclimates of extreme south Florida or greenhouse cultivation.

directions: Musang King (registered as clone D197 in Malaysia) is currently the most sought-after commercial durian cultivar in the world, commanding premium export prices for its thick, deep-yellow to golden flesh, small seed, and rich, custardy, bittersweet flavor with a lingering finish. Trees need deep, fertile, well-drained soil, high humidity, and warm temperatures year-round; flowers open at night and rely heavily on bats and other nocturnal pollinators, so avoid dusk pesticide use and encourage nearby night-pollinator habitat. Fruit takes roughly 3-5 months to mature after flowering, and the heavy spiny husks should be allowed to fall naturally rather than being cut, both for safety and because Musang King is known to ripen poorly if harvested green. As with all durian, plant only where extended winter cold is not a risk.
sources: Malaysian Department of Agriculture -- Durian Clone Registration
TFNet (International Tropical Fruits Network) -- Durian Varieties
University of Hawaii CTAHR -- Durian for Hawaii

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in a humid, frost-free tropical climate; Monthong needs the same consistent warmth above 50F as other durian and is realistically limited to the most tropical microclimates of extreme south Florida or greenhouse cultivation.

directions: Monthong (Thai for 'golden pillow') is Thailand's leading commercial durian cultivar and the variety most commonly exported worldwide, known for large fruit, thick pale-yellow flesh, a relatively mild odor and sweetness compared to other cultivars, and a small proportion of seed to flesh. Grow in deep, fertile, well-drained soil with high humidity and warm year-round temperatures; the tree flowers at night and depends primarily on bats for pollination, so avoid pesticide applications near dusk. Fruit develops over roughly 3-5 months and should be left to drop naturally rather than cut from the tree, both for safety around the spiny husk and for proper ripening. Monthong trees are large and long-lived, eventually reaching great size where climate allows sustained outdoor growth.
sources: TFNet (International Tropical Fruits Network) -- Durian Varieties
University of Hawaii CTAHR -- Durian for Hawaii
Thailand Department of Agriculture -- Durian Cultivar Notes

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in a humid, frost-free tropical climate; D24 needs the same consistent warmth above 50F as other durian and is realistically limited to the most tropical microclimates of extreme south Florida or greenhouse cultivation.

directions: D24, also marketed as Sultan, is one of Malaysia's oldest and most widely recommended commercial durian clones, valued for a distinctive bitter-sweet flavor balance, creamy pale-yellow flesh, and consistently good yields that made it an industry benchmark before Musang King's rise in popularity. Grow in deep, fertile, well-drained soil with abundant humidity and stable warm temperatures; flowering occurs at night and pollination depends heavily on bats, so avoid disturbing nocturnal pollinators with pesticides near dusk. Fruit matures roughly 3-5 months after flowering and should be allowed to fall naturally, since the heavy spined husk makes hand-cutting hazardous and premature harvest results in poor flavor development. D24 remains a common choice for growers wanting a well-documented, reliable cultivar alongside newer premium selections.
sources: Malaysian Department of Agriculture -- Durian Clone Registration
TFNet (International Tropical Fruits Network) -- Durian Varieties
University of Hawaii CTAHR -- Durian for Hawaii

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in a humid, frost-free tropical climate; Chanee needs the same consistent warmth above 50F as other durian and is realistically limited to the most tropical microclimates of extreme south Florida or greenhouse cultivation.

directions: Chanee (registered in Malaysia as D123 and grown widely in Thailand as well) is one of the earliest-fruiting and most productive durian cultivars, popular with growers for its precocious bearing, consistent annual cropping, and moderately sweet, fiber-free flesh. Because it fruits reliably at a younger tree age than many other cultivars, Chanee is often recommended as a starter or trial cultivar in new durian plantings. Grow in deep, fertile, well-drained soil with high humidity and steady warm temperatures, protecting flowers from pesticide disturbance since durian relies on nocturnal bat pollination. Allow the spiny husks to drop naturally rather than cutting them, both for safety and because the fruit continues to develop sugars right up to natural fall.
sources: Malaysian Department of Agriculture -- Durian Clone Registration
TFNet (International Tropical Fruits Network) -- Durian Varieties
University of Hawaii CTAHR -- Durian for Hawaii

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in a humid, frost-free tropical climate; Black Thorn, registered as clone D200, requires the same consistent warmth above 50F as other durian and is realistically limited to the most tropical microclimates of extreme south Florida or greenhouse cultivation.

directions: Black Thorn (clone D200), named for the dark bases of its thorny husk spines, is a premium Malaysian durian cultivar that rivals Musang King in price and reputation, prized for an unusually small seed, thick flesh, and a rich, dense, custardy texture with a distinct bittersweet, almost boozy depth of flavor. It is a relatively slow, low-yielding cultivar compared to older commercial clones, which contributes to its scarcity and high value. Grow in deep, fertile, well-drained soil with consistently high humidity and warm temperatures, and protect flowering periods from pesticide disturbance since pollination depends on nocturnal bats. As with all durian, allow the heavy spined fruit to fall naturally, and plant only in genuinely frost-free, humid tropical conditions.
sources: Malaysian Department of Agriculture -- Durian Clone Registration
TFNet (International Tropical Fruits Network) -- Durian Varieties
kingofdurian.com -- Durian Clone Reference
